quote: Reality just seems to go on crunching through General Relativity, even when it only makes a difference at the fourteenth decimal place, which a human would regard as a huge waste of computing power. Physics does it with brute force. No one has ever caught physics simplifying its calculations
content: Physicists do not believe that reality “crunches through General Relativity.” General relativity is not unified with quantum mechanics, fails at the Planck scale, and is generally regarded as an effective field theory, the low-energy limit of something else (Donoghue (1994)), which is to say it stands to the true dynamics roughly as Newton stands to it. The essay’s example of the single level that reality really uses is a level that the field expects to be an approximation. The metaphor is also a case of the fallacy the essay is named for: “physics does it with brute force,” “no one has ever caught physics simplifying its calculations,” “I wish I knew where Reality got its computing power” (in Reductionism) all picture the universe as a computer running a program, and a computer running a program is a mind-shaped thing. Nothing in physics says that nature calculates; the equations are our description, and whether the description’s cost of evaluation corresponds to anything in the world is precisely the question that separates the map from the territory. The essay’s reductionism is stated in the vocabulary of the mind projection it is meant to exclude.

quote: It seems to me that a word like “snow” or “white” can be taken as a kind of promissory note—not a known specification of exactly which physical quark configurations count as “snow,” but, nonetheless, there are things you call snow and things you don’t call snow, and even if you got a few items wrong (like plastic snow), an Ideal Omniscient Science Interpreter would see a tight cluster in the center and redraw the boundary to have a simpler definition.
content: Book III’s annotations found that “simple boundaries in Thingspace” had no description language and hence no content; here the same device is the theory of reference. “Simpler definition” is relative to a vocabulary, and Goodman’s grue shows that the world does not supply one: what is a tight cluster in one basis is scattered in another. The Interpreter’s redrawn boundary around “snow” will include or exclude hail, frost, rime, névé and firn depending on whether the interest is meteorological, glaciological or recreational, and no quark configuration decides that. This is the qua problem for causal theories of reference (Devitt and Sterelny, Language and Reality, 1987), and Putnam’s own answer, which the essay cites without using, is that reference is fixed by the environment together with the linguistic community and its division of labour, not by an omniscient simplifier. The promissory-note picture is a version of the causal-descriptive theory and it is a reasonable one; its “simplicity” clause is the part that does the work, and it is the part the book has never been able to cash.

quote: But then, the entire grasp that we have upon reality is made up of promissory notes of this kind. So, rather than calling it circular, I prefer to call it self-consistent.
content: Renaming the circle does not straighten it, and the problem has a name and a literature. Alston’s The Reliability of Sense Perception (1993) showed that every doxastic practice, sense perception, memory, the telescope, can be certified reliable only by using its own outputs, so that “reflective coherence” is available to any practice that is internally consistent, including ones that are wrong; a community of tarot readers whose readings confirm one another is self-consistent in the essay’s sense. Alston’s conclusion is that epistemic circularity is unavoidable and that one is rational to trust socially established practices that are not internally incoherent, which is a modest position the essay could adopt. What the essay does instead is to treat “self-consistent” as a term of praise that distinguishes the telescope from introspection, when the argument it gives applies equally to both. The Smullyan quotation concedes the point in advance: the statement is credited with not being inconsistent, and nothing more, and “nothing more” is what Alston said too.
